sourceCourseTitle: Llm Application Security Red Teaming Specialist / Prompt Injection and Output Handling

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How direct and indirect prompt injection work and why they succeed 2) How to recognize attacker patterns and high-risk inputs 3) Practical defenses for input/output handling, isolation, and least-privilege tool use

blocks.title: Stop Prompt Injection, Guardrail Bypass & Output Leakage
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
Prompt injection is an adversarial attempt to override or subvert a model’s intended behavior. Direct injection occurs when an attacker places instructions in the same channel the model reads as authoritative (e.g., user input: "Ignore previous instructions and …").

Indirect injection occurs when malicious instructions are embedded in external or retrieved content (web pages, PDFs, emails, tool outputs, file metadata) that the model is asked to process. Typical attacker goals include: instruction override (e.g., changing task goals), data exfiltration (e.g., "reveal secrets"), policy evasion (e.g., jailbreaks), and tool abuse (e.g., triggering external actions).

Key risks arise from instruction ambiguity and misplaced trust in untrusted content. Models are trained to be helpful and can treat content as instructions rather than data.

This is amplified in agentic systems where the model can call tools, browse, or write files, turning a prompt failure into system-level impact. Defenses rely on defense-in-depth: treat all retrieved or user-supplied content as untrusted data; clearly separate instructions (system) from data (user/context) and reinforce role boundaries; use allowlists for tools and arguments, with server-side validation; sandbox side effects (network, file system); parse-then-validate outputs using strict schemas; apply content sanitization (strip or neutralize instruction-like patterns, HTML comments, and hidden text); implement refusal rules for following instructions originating from content; use provenance signals and content labeling; reduce model privilege (least privilege, scoped API keys) and implement approval gates for sensitive actions.

• Direct injection: Adversarial instructions entered directly into the chat to override goals or policies.
• Indirect injection: Malicious instructions hidden in external content (web pages, documents, tool outputs) that the model processes.
• Defense-in-depth: Treat untrusted inputs as data, enforce allowlists and validation for tools, sandbox side effects, and require structured, validated outputs.

• Direct injection comes from the user; indirect injection hides in external content the model processes.
• The highest risks are instruction override, data exfiltration, and tool abuse.
• Defend with role separation, sanitization, structured outputs, allowlisted tools, validation, and sandboxed side effects.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core injection types and how to mitigate them with robust input/output handling and least-privilege design.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) What system prompt leakage is and why it matters 2) Common leakage vectors, including indirect prompts, tool outputs, and logs 3) Prevention, detection, and response strategies (canaries, redaction, output filtering, and compartmentalization)

The system prompt defines the model’s role, constraints, and policies. Leakage occurs when the model exposes all or part of that hidden context (or secrets referenced by it) to users or external systems.

Leak channels include: direct requests ("show me your instructions"), jailbreaks, indirect injection via retrieved content that asks the model to reveal hidden context, verbose error messages, tool outputs that echo prompt text, and analytics/logging that surface sensitive content. Risks escalate when the system prompt contains sensitive data (API keys, internal URLs, credentials, model routing rules).

Best practice is to never embed secrets in prompts. Instead, keep secrets server-side and expose them only through controlled tools/functions with scoped credentials and argument validation.

Mitigations: avoid secrets in prompts; compartmentalize prompts across tasks/agents; add explicit refusal rules and output filters that block disclosure of internal instructions and tokens; mask/redact identifiers in tool outputs and logs; use canary strings in the system prompt for detection and alerting; limit model self-inspection abilities; constrain memory persistence; and regularly red-team for leak paths. If leakage is detected, rotate credentials, update prompts to remove sensitive content, and adjust controls that allowed exposure.

blocks.title: AI Model Penetration: Testing LLMs for Prompt Injection
blocks.label: Recommended Viewing

body.en:
• System prompts vs. secrets: Never place credentials in prompts; use server-side tools with scoped tokens.
• Leakage channels: Direct queries, indirect injection via content, verbose errors, tool outputs, and logging/analytics.
• Prevent and detect: Refusal policies, output filtering, compartmentalization, canary strings, and rapid credential rotation on exposure.

• Never store secrets in system prompts; route sensitive access through server-side tools with scoped credentials.
• Leakage can occur through direct queries, indirect injection, tool outputs, and logs; monitor with canary strings and filters.
• On exposure, rotate credentials, remove sensitive content from prompts, and harden output and tool controls.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand system prompt leakage risks and how to prevent, detect, and respond to them in production systems.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) Why LLM outputs must be treated as untrusted input and common failure modes (e.g., command, HTML/Markdown, CSV/Excel, URL, and file-path injections).
- 2) How to safely consume model outputs using strict schemas, allowlists, escaping/sanitization, sandboxing, and confirmation flows.
- 3) Practical red-team tests and monitoring techniques to detect and prevent insecure output handling issues.

LLM outputs often drive downstream actions: rendered UI, executed commands, HTTP requests, file operations, or database queries. Treat every model output as untrusted data until validated. Insecure output handling occurs when an application directly trusts and executes, renders, or forwards model text without guardrails, enabling XSS in UIs, shell/SQL injection, SSRF via model-suggested URLs, path traversal, or malicious spreadsheet formulas.

Defenses center on strict interfaces and least privilege. Use structured outputs (e.g., JSON schemas) and reject or repair non-conforming responses. For command generation, parse into a safe AST and enforce allowlists of subcommands and arguments; require user confirmation and dry-run diffs for destructive actions; execute in a sandbox with limited privileges. When rendering content, use a Markdown renderer that disables raw HTML and sanitize with an allowlist-based HTML sanitizer; add a strong Content Security Policy (CSP). For CSV/Excel, prefix dangerous formulas or escape leading =, +, -, and @. For URLs and network calls, resolve and validate against an allowlist, block private IP ranges, and perform server-side fetches with stripped headers. Constrain file access to a chroot/workspace and canonicalize paths to prevent traversal. Log and monitor outputs and policy decisions for forensics and continuous improvement.

• Untrusted-by-default: Never directly execute, render, or forward model output without validation.
• Structured validation: Enforce strict JSON schemas/ASTs, allowlists, and type checks; reject or repair.
• Side-effect controls: Escape/sanitize for UI, sandbox execution, confirmation for risky ops, network and file system restrictions.

• Treat all LLM outputs as untrusted; validate against strict schemas and policies.
• Escape/sanitize for UI rendering and neutralize CSV/Excel formulas; enforce CSP.
• Constrain side effects with allowlists, sandboxing, confirmations, and network/file system restrictions.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to safely consume LLM outputs and prevent exploitation via insecure output handling.

blocks.title: Microsoft AI Red Teaming Labs Full Course (Part 1)
blocks.label: Tutorial

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How prompt isolation separates roles, contexts, and untrusted data to resist prompt injection and cross-contamination.
- 2) How to design and operate independent policy layers that gate inputs, outputs, and tool use regardless of prompt wording.
- 3) Practical architectures and tests for RAG, multi-agent systems, and tool-enabled agents that prevent untrusted content from gaining unintended authority.

Prompt isolation ensures that untrusted content (e.g., retrieved web pages, user uploads) is processed in compartments that do not have authority to perform sensitive actions. Use separate roles or even separate models: a "reader" or retriever model without tool access transforms raw content into a neutral, structured summary; a separate executor agent with restricted tools acts only on that summary under policy. Never let untrusted text write into system prompts or tool instructions.

A policy layer is an independent gate that inspects inputs, planned tool calls, and outputs against deterministic rules and safety/business constraints. Examples include allow/deny lists for tools, argument validators, PII/secret redaction, DLP checks, and refusal/justification policies. Policies should be enforced out-of-band from the model (e.g., middleware) and produce auditable decisions.

Key practices: tag data with provenance (source, trust level, tenant) and preserve it through the pipeline; restrict capabilities based on provenance; use per-tenant memory/vector-store namespaces and scoped credentials; limit context sharing across sessions; add self-check or verifier models that critique actions against policy; and employ sandboxes/timeouts/quotas for any code execution. For RAG, treat retrieved text as data only: strip scripts, normalize, and strictly template prompts so that untrusted content cannot alter instructions.

• Role and context separation: Process untrusted content in compartments with no tool authority; pass only structured, minimal summaries forward.
• Independent policy layer: Middleware that validates inputs/outputs/tool calls (allowlists, argument checks, DLP/PII rules) regardless of prompt phrasing.
• Provenance and tenancy: Tag data with source/tenant and enforce per-tenant isolation for memories, indices, and credentials.

• Separate untrusted content from authority: compartmentalize roles and never grant tools to channels that ingest untrusted text.
• Enforce an independent policy layer to validate and gate actions, inputs, and outputs.
• Preserve provenance and tenant boundaries across memory, indices, and credentials.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to isolate prompts and enforce policies that make LLM applications resilient to prompt injection.
